records.quote: Corollary 4.2 Let Xλ1, Xλ2, . . . , Xλn be independent random variables with Xλi ∼ W(α, λi), where λi > 0, i = 1, . . . , n, and let Xθ1, Xθ2, . . . , Xθn be another set of independent random variables with Xθi ∼ W(α, θi), where θi > 0, i = 1, . . . , n. Then for 0 < α ≤ 1, (λ1, . . . , λn) ≼m (θ1, . . . , θn) ⇒ Xλn:n ≤rh Xθn:n.
records.family: Weibull W(α, λ), common shape α, heterogeneous scale parameters λi
records.compared: Xλn:n (scale vector λ) vs Xθn:n (scale vector θ)

hypotheses.formal: λ majorized by θ (Definition 2.2: equal sums and Σ_{i=1}^j λ_(i) ≥ Σ_{i=1}^j θ_(i), j = 1,...,n−1)

conclusion.direction: Xλn:n ≤rh Xθn:n (λ-system smaller in reversed hazard rate order)

records.ambiguity: Immediate from Theorem 4.1 since ≼m ⇒ ≼w. Pass A's 'hr' label is wrong — the paper prints ≤rh (reverse hazard rate order). Note in text: proved earlier by Khaledi et al. (2011) for generalized gamma with p = q < 1.

note: Disputed hr (A) vs rh (B). The paper prints ≤rh — the reversed hazard rate order; corrected to rh.

Pass A only. Lemma 3.1 proves convexity/monotonicity of the auxiliary function u(t) = αt^α/(e^{t^α}−1) for 0 < α ≤ 1 — an analytic function property used in the proofs, with no ordering conclusion between distributions. Out of spec scope.
Pass A only. Lemma 3.2 proves monotonicity of v(t) = t^α/(1−e^{−t^α}) for 0 < α ≤ 1 — analytic function property, no distributional ordering. Out of spec scope.
Pass A only. Lemma 3.3 proves ψ3(t) = te^t(1+t−e^t)/(e^t−1)^3 is increasing — analytic function property, no distributional ordering. Out of spec scope.
Pass A only. Lemma 3.4 proves w(t) = αt^{α−1}ψ3(t^α) is increasing for 0 < α ≤ 1 — analytic function property, no distributional ordering. Out of spec scope.

records.quote: Theorem 4.1 Let Xλ1, Xλ2, . . . , Xλn be independent random variables with Xλi ∼ W(α, λi), where λi > 0, i = 1, . . . , n, and let Xθ1, Xθ2, . . . , Xθn be another set of independent random variables with Xθi ∼ W(α, θi), where θi > 0, i = 1, . . . , n. Then for 0 < α ≤ 1, (λ1, . . . , λn) ≼w (θ1, . . . , θn) ⇒ Xλn:n ≤rh Xθn:n.
records.family: Weibull W(α, λ), common shape α, heterogeneous scale parameters λi
records.compared: Xλn:n (scale vector λ) vs Xθn:n (scale vector θ)

hypotheses.formal: λ weakly majorized by θ in the paper's sense (Definition 2.4: Σ_{i=1}^j λ_(i) ≥ Σ_{i=1}^j θ_(i) for all j — i.e. weak supermajorization)

conclusion.direction: Xλn:n ≤rh Xθn:n (λ-system smaller in reversed hazard rate order)

records.ambiguity: Pass A's 'hr' label is wrong — the paper prints ≤rh. The paper's ≼w (Definition 2.4) is the lower-partial-sum ≥ relation (weak supermajorization in Marshall–Olkin terminology).

note: Disputed hr (A) vs rh (B). The paper prints ≤rh — reversed hazard rate order under weak supermajorization of scale vectors; corrected to rh.

records.quote: Theorem 4.12 Let X1, . . . , Xn be independent random variables following the multiple-outlier Weibull model such that Xi ∼ W(α, λ1) for i = 1, . . . , p and Xj ∼ W(α, λ) for j = p + 1, . . . , n, with λ1, λ > 0. Let Y1, . . . , Yn be another set of independent random variables following the multiple-outlier Weibull model with Yi ∼ W(α, λ*1) for i = 1, . . . , p and Yj ∼ W(α, λ) for j = p + 1, . . . , n, with λ*1, λ > 0. Suppose λ*1 = min(λ, λ1, λ*1), then for any α > 0, (λ1,...,λ1,λ,...,λ)p,q ≼w (λ*1,...,λ*1,λ,...,λ)p,q ⇒ r*n:n(t)/rn:n(t) is increasing in t, where p + q = n.
records.family: multiple-outlier Weibull model W(α, ·): X has p components at λ1 and q at λ; Y has p components at λ*1 and q at λ
records.compared: Xn:n (p outliers at λ1) vs Yn:n (p outliers at λ*1); common shape α, common λ-block

hypotheses.formal: λ*1 ≤ min(λ, λ1) — the outlier scale of Y is the smallest of the three values
weak supermajorization (Definition 2.4) between the two-value scale vectors

conclusion.direction: Xn:n ages faster than Yn:n in the reversed hazard rate sense: r̃Yn:n(t)/r̃Xn:n(t) = r*n:n(t)/rn:n(t) is increasing in t

records.quantifiers: p + q = n; all t ≥ 0; any α > 0
records.ambiguity: Conclusion is the rh-ratio monotonicity (relative-ageing ≲rhr) condition of Shaked–Shanthikumar Thm 1.C.4(b) used to lift ≤rh to ≤lr in Theorem 4.13 — neither a plain hr (pass A) nor plain rh (pass B) order. Pass A's quote rendered λ*1 as λ−1 (mis-OCR); the paper prints λ*1, the smaller outlier scale.

note: Disputed hr (A) vs rh (B). Neither is exact: the printed conclusion is that the ratio r*_{n:n}(t)/r_{n:n}(t) of reversed hazard rates is increasing — the reversed-hazard relative-ageing relation, canonically 'ageing: rhr'. Also corrects A's λ−1 → λ*1.

records.quote: Theorem 4.3 Let Xλ1, Xλ2 be independent random variables with Xλi ∼ W(α, λi) where λi > 0, i = 1, 2, and let Xθ1, Xθ2 be independent random variables with Xθi ∼ W(α, θi) where θi > 0, i = 1, 2. Then (λ1, λ2) ≼m (θ1, θ2) ⇒ rθ2:2(t)/rλ2:2(t) is increasing in t, for 0 < α ≤ 1.
records.family: Weibull W(α, λ), common shape α, n = 2 heterogeneous scale parameters
records.compared: Xλ2:2 (scales λ1, λ2) vs Xθ2:2 (scales θ1, θ2)

conclusion.direction: Xλ2:2 ages faster than Xθ2:2 in the reversed hazard rate sense: r̃Xθ2:2(t)/r̃Xλ2:2(t) increasing in t

records.ambiguity: Ratio-monotonicity conclusion (r̃^θ_{2:2}/r̃^λ_{2:2} increasing) — the rh relative-ageing condition feeding Theorem 1.C.4 to lift ≤rh to ≤lr in Theorem 4.4; neither plain hr (A) nor plain rh (B).

note: Disputed hr (A) vs rh (B). Printed conclusion is monotonicity of the reversed-hazard-rate ratio — canonically 'ageing: rhr', the ≲rhr relative-ageing relation.

records.quote: Theorem 4.4 Let Xλ1, Xλ2 be independent random variables with Xλi ∼ W(α, λi) where λi > 0, i = 1, 2, and let Xθ1, Xθ2 be independent random variables with Xθi ∼ W(α, θi) where θi > 0, i = 1, 2. Then for 0 < α ≤ 1, (λ1, λ2) ≼m (θ1, θ2) ⇒ Xλ2:2 ≤lr Xθ2:2.
records.family: Weibull W(α, λ), common shape α, n = 2 heterogeneous scale parameters

conclusion.direction: Xλ2:2 ≤lr Xθ2:2 (λ-system smaller in likelihood ratio order)

records.ambiguity: Via Theorems 4.1 + 4.3 and Shaked–Shanthikumar Thm 1.C.4. Generalizes Dykstra et al. (1997) Thm 3.1 from exponential to Weibull. Example 4.5 shows the result fails for α = 2.

note: Both passes agree: lr ordering for n = 2 under majorization, 0 < α ≤ 1. Direction X^λ_{2:2} ≤lr X^θ_{2:2} as printed.

records.quote: Theorem 4.6 Let X1, . . . , Xn be independent random variables following the multiple-outlier Weibull model such that Xi ∼ W(α, λ1) for i = 1, . . . , p and Xj ∼ W(α, λ2) for j = p + 1, . . . , n, with λ1, λ2 > 0. Let Y1, . . . , Yn be another set of independent random variables following the multiple-outlier Weibull model such that Yi ∼ W(α, θ1) for i = 1, . . . , p and Yj ∼ W(α, θ2) for j = p + 1, . . . , n, with θ1, θ2 > 0. Then for 0 < α ≤ 1, (λ1,...,λ1,λ2,...,λ2)p,q ≼m (θ1,...,θ1,θ2,...,θ2)p,q ⇒ rθn:n(t)/rλn:n(t) is increasing in t, where p + q = n.
records.family: multiple-outlier Weibull model W(α, ·): p components at first scale, q at second
records.compared: Xn:n (scales λ1^p, λ2^q) vs Yn:n (scales θ1^p, θ2^q)

hypotheses.text: (λ1,...,λ1,λ2,...,λ2) ≼m (θ1,...,θ1,θ2,...,θ2) with p and q copies, p + q = n
hypotheses.formal: majorization (Definition 2.2) between the two multiple-outlier scale vectors

conclusion.direction: Xn:n ages faster than Yn:n in the reversed hazard rate sense: r̃Yn:n(t)/r̃Xn:n(t) = rθn:n(t)/rλn:n(t) increasing in t

records.ambiguity: Ratio-monotonicity (rh relative-ageing) conclusion lifting Theorem 4.1's ≤rh to ≤lr via Thm 1.C.4 in Theorem 4.7; neither plain hr (A) nor plain rh (B).

note: Disputed hr (A) vs rh (B). Printed conclusion is monotonicity of the reversed-hazard-rate ratio — canonically 'ageing: rhr'.

records.quote: Theorem 4.7 Let X1, . . . , Xn be independent random variables following the multiple-outlier Weibull model such that Xi ∼ W(α, λ1) for i = 1, . . . , p and Xj ∼ W(α, λ2) for j = p + 1, . . . , n, with λ1, λ2 > 0. Let Y1, . . . , Yn be another set of independent random variables following the multiple-outlier Weibull model such that Yi ∼ W(α, θ1) for i = 1, . . . , p and Yj ∼ W(α, θ2) for j = p + 1, . . . , n, with θ1, θ2 > 0. Then for 0 < α ≤ 1, (λ1,...,λ1,λ2,...,λ2)p,q ≼m (θ1,...,θ1,θ2,...,θ2)p,q ⇒ Xλn:n ≤lr Xθn:n, where p + q = n.
records.family: multiple-outlier Weibull model W(α, ·): p components at first scale, q at second
records.compared: Xλn:n (scales λ1^p, λ2^q) vs Xθn:n (scales θ1^p, θ2^q)

hypotheses.text: (λ1,...,λ1,λ2,...,λ2) ≼m (θ1,...,θ1,θ2,...,θ2) with p and q copies, p + q = n
hypotheses.formal: majorization (Definition 2.2) between the two multiple-outlier scale vectors

conclusion.direction: Xλn:n ≤lr Xθn:n (λ-system smaller in likelihood ratio order)

records.ambiguity: Via Theorems 4.1 + 4.6 and Shaked–Shanthikumar Thm 1.C.4. Paper glosses: more dispersed scale parameters (majorization) give a stochastically larger parallel-system maximum.

note: Both passes agree on lr; direction X^λ_{n:n} ≤lr X^θ_{n:n} as printed under majorization of scale vectors, 0 < α ≤ 1.

records.quote: Theorem 4.8 Let Xλ1, Xλ be independent random variables with Xλ1 ∼ W(α, λ1) and Xλ ∼ W(α, λ) where λ1, λ > 0. Let Yλ*1, Yλ be independent random variables with Yλ*1 ∼ W(α, λ*1) and Yλ ∼ W(α, λ), where λ*1, λ > 0. Suppose λ*1 = min(λ, λ1, λ*1), then for any α > 0, (λ1, λ) ≼w (λ*1, λ) ⇒ r*2:2(t)/r2:2(t) is increasing in t.
records.family: Weibull W(α, ·), n = 2: X = (λ1, λ), Y = (λ*1, λ) — only the first scale differs
records.compared: X2:2 (scales λ1, λ) vs Y2:2 (scales λ*1, λ)

hypotheses.formal: λ*1 ≤ min(λ, λ1) — Y's outlier scale is the smallest

conclusion.direction: X2:2 ages faster than Y2:2 in the reversed hazard rate sense: r̃Y2:2(t)/r̃X2:2(t) = r*2:2(t)/r2:2(t) increasing in t

records.ambiguity: Ratio-monotonicity conclusion for Theorem 4.9 via Thm 1.C.4; valid only when the distinct scale λ*1 is the minimum (the third arrangement λ ≤ λ*1 ≤ λ1 fails — Example 4.10). Neither plain hr (A) nor plain rh (B).

note: Disputed hr (A) vs rh (B). Printed conclusion is monotonicity of the reversed-hazard-rate ratio — canonically 'ageing: rhr'; restricted to λ*1 = min, any α > 0.

records.quote: Theorem 4.9 Let Xλ1, Xλ be independent random variables with Xλ1 ∼ W(α, λ1) and Xλ ∼ W(α, λ) where λ1, λ > 0. Let Yλ*1, Yλ be independent random variables with Yλ*1 ∼ W(α, λ*1) and Yλ ∼ W(α, λ), where λ*1, λ > 0. Suppose λ*1 = min(λ, λ1, λ*1), then for any α > 0, (λ1, λ) ≼w (λ*1, λ) ⇒ X2:2 ≤lr Y2:2.

records.compared: X2:2 (scales λ1, λ) vs Y2:2 (scales λ*1, λ)

hypotheses.formal: λ*1 ≤ min(λ, λ1) — covers λ*1 ≤ λ ≤ λ1 and λ*1 ≤ λ1 ≤ λ; excludes λ ≤ λ*1 ≤ λ1

conclusion.direction: X2:2 ≤lr Y2:2 (X-system smaller in likelihood ratio order)

records.ambiguity: Via Theorem 4.8 + Theorem 4.1 (≤rh) + Shaked–Shanthikumar Thm 1.C.4. The third possible arrangement λ ≤ λ*1 ≤ λ1 is explicitly excluded and refuted by Example 4.10 (α = 0.3 and α = 1.3 figures).

note: Both passes agree: lr ordering for n = 2 under weak supermajorization with the smallest-scale constraint, valid for any α > 0.
